extracted.intended_audience: senior undergraduate or graduate students in theory of computation / computability theory
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-week textbook project for an advanced undergraduate/graduate theory course asking students to (a) state and compare Turing and Kleene definitions of computability and prove basic closure properties, and (b) study Shepherdson’s construction converting two-way DFAs to one-way DFAs by computing ‘effects’ of prefixes and implementing the mechanical construction (programming tasks included).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleene’s definition of multivariable Turing computable functions
rubrics_metrics.description: State in your own words Kleene’s definition of Turing computable functions of multiple variables. Kleene mentions that the representation of the tuple x1; : : : ; xn on a tape requires x1 1 squares. Explain why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Kleene’s remark (excerpted from Kleene [11]) and the textbook discussion: explain how n-tuples of naturals are encoded on a Turing tape in 'standard position', why the tape needs a specified number of squares to represent the tuple, and how this relates to the machine stopping with the n+1-tuple scanned in standard position. Give an informal but precise justification for the claimed number of tape squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of Turing’s and Kleene’s one-variable definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Are Turing’s and Kleene’s definitions of computable functions of one variable equivalent? Explain why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear argument showing simulation/translation between the two formulations for one-variable functions, citing how machines and recursive definitions correspond. Use examples if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of generalized Turing computability to Kleene’s multivariable definition (extra credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Extra Credit) Is your generalization of Turing computability to functions of multiple variables equivalent to Kleene’s definition of computable functions of multiple variables? Explain why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a proof or sketch that your chosen generalization for multivariable Turing computability matches Kleene’s formulation (or explain any discrepancies). Address encoding/decoding of tuples and halting/partiality issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successor is Turing computable
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the successor function s(x) = x + 1 is Turing computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe or exhibit a Turing machine (or finite-state procedure in the chosen encoding) that, given a representation of x, produces the representation of x+1 and halts. Provide enough detail to convince the reader that the operation is computable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant functions are Turing computable
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the constant functions f(x1,...,xn) = c are Turing computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how a machine can ignore input and produce the fixed output c in the chosen tape representation, handling arity and standard-position conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity projections are Turing computable
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the identity functions U^j_n(x1,...,xn) = xj are Turing computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe a machine that, given an encoded n-tuple, selects the j-th component and leaves/outputs it in the required representation; account for tape-format and head-position details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution schema preserves Turing computability
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why, whenever g(.x1,...,xm/) and h1(.x1,...,xn/),...,hm(.x1,...,xn/) are Turing computable, then f(.x1,...,xn/) defined by f(x) = g(h1(x),...,hm(x)) is also Turing computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue by construction: show how to build a machine that computes the hi's from the input, arranges their outputs appropriately, and then computes g on those outputs. Address partiality (undefined values) and standard encoding conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive recursion preserves Turing computability
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why, whenever g(.x1,...,xn/) and h(.x1,...,xn, y/) are Turing computable, then f defined by primitive recursion is Turing computable (i.e., f(0,x2,...,xn)=g(x2,...,xn) and f(k+1,x2,...,xn)=h(k,f(k,x2,...,xn),x2,...,xn)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a construction or simulation argument for a machine that implements primitive recursion via iteration, showing how intermediate values are stored and used, and handling termination/partiality conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleene’s μ-operator preserves Turing computability
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why, whenever R(x1,...,xn,y) is Turing computable and some boundedness/totality condition holds, then the μ-operator applied to R yields a Turing computable function (as described in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how a machine can perform the unbounded/minimum search (or bounded search under the given hypothesis), how it detects the predicate R being satisfied, and how partiality is managed. Reference the textual definition of Kleene’s μ-operator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of primitive/general recursive functions to Church’s thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Using exercises 5.(a)–5.(f) make a deduction concerning primitive recursive and general recursive functions. How is your conclusion related to Church’s thesis?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the closure/completeness results established in previous subexercises and explain how they support the identification of computable functions (e.g., showing every Turing-computable function is general recursive or vice versa), and relate that to the informal content of Church’s thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate A1 accepting 11001010
rubrics_metrics.description: [1] Demonstrate the steps performed by A1 in accepting the tape 11001010.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the sequence of configurations (state, head position, and tape contents) showing how A1 scans and transitions to acceptance (moves and intermediate states). The textbook gives the 10-state transition table; use it to produce the step-by-step run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate A1 processing 11001001 and conclude rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: [2] Demonstrate the steps performed by A1 in processing the tape 11001001. Conclude that the tape is not accepted by A1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce the run (configurations) on input 11001001 using A1’s table, show why the machine fails to move off the right-hand edge in an accepting state, and conclude non-acceptance (may stop without required scanned n+1-tuple or loop).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate A2 accepting 101001
rubrics_metrics.description: [3] Demonstrate that the input 101001 is accepted by A2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use A2’s transition table to trace the machine’s run on 101001 and show that it eventually moves off the right-hand edge in an accepting state. Provide intermediate states and head moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate A2 non-acceptance on 10111 (infinite loop)
rubrics_metrics.description: [4] Demonstrate that the input 10111 is not accepted by A2. Indeed, A2 will run into an infinite loop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the computation to show the repeating configuration or behavior that yields a non-terminating run; explain why no accepting move off the right edge occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute 'effect' of a prefix (Shepherdson construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and compute the 'effect' of an input prefix t: (1) the state in which the 2DFA exits t when started at q0 on its leftmost square, and (2) for each possible state q in which t might later be re-entered, the state q' in which the machine would leave t again (the external effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Shepherdson’s description: represent the external effect as tuples like [(q1,R), (q2,L), ...], and show how these two pieces of information determine how a one-way machine can carry forward the table of question-answer combinations. Use the worked examples for prefixes 1, 10, 101 to illustrate computation of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute effects iteratively to decide acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: [5] From the effect of a prefix and the transition table, compute the effect of the prefix extended by one symbol (e.g., extend 10 by 1 to get 101) and use repeated extension to determine acceptance of a full input (e.g., 101001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the step-by-step computation of new effect tuples from previous ones and the transition table without knowledge of the raw prefix; demonstrate how final effect indicates acceptance. Provide the explicit effects shown in the text for examples (e.g., effect of 1, 10, 101, 101001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use effect computations to show acceptance/non-acceptance for example inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: [6][7] Repeatedly compute effects extending 101 by 0,0,1 to conclude 101001 is accepted, and repeat for 10111 to conclude it is not accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform the iterative effect updates as in the previous item for both example inputs, recording each intermediate effect; conclude acceptance or non-acceptance based on the final effect and the acceptance condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count distinct effects and DFA states needed
rubrics_metrics.description: [8] How many different effects can there be in simulating A2 by a DFA? How many states are needed for a DFA to accept the same set of inputs as A2?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that only finitely many different effects exist (since Q is finite) and compute the number (or give an upper bound) combinatorially; deduce the required number of DFA states (equal to number of distinct effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Shepherdson’s method to A1 and compute DFA size
rubrics_metrics.description: [9] Applying Shepherdson’s method to A1, how many states are there in the DFA constructed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either perform the mechanical construction by hand (tedious) or write a program to compute all effects for prefixes and count distinct effects. The text notes the smallest DFA accepting the same set as A1 has 33 states (use as a check).

rubrics_metrics.name: Program the Shepherdson construction (mechanical computation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement a program to perform the computation of effects and the mechanical construction of a DFA equivalent to a given 2DFA (compute distinct effects and produce DFA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook recommends writing a program due to tedium; the program should take a 2DFA description (states, transition function) and enumerate effects for prefixes to produce the equivalent DFA and count states. Use provided examples (A1–A4) as test cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct DFA equivalent to 2DFA-with-endmarkers A3 and compare sizes with/without markers
rubrics_metrics.description: [10] For A3 (2DFA-with-endmarkers), explain the construction of a DFA equivalent to A3 accepting inputs delimited by b and e; compute how many states the DFA has. Then modify the DFA to accept inputs with the endmarkers b and e removed and determine the change in number of states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Shepherdson’s extension to machines with explicit endmarkers. Construct effect tuples that include marker behavior, count distinct effects, and note the textbook remark that the smallest DFA accepting the same set without endmarkers has 64 states (use as check).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat endmarker construction for A4
rubrics_metrics.description: [11] Re-do part [10] for A4 (2DFA-with-endmarkers A4): construct equivalent DFA(s) and determine state counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform the same mechanical/programmatic construction as for A3. The text again notes the smallest DFA accepting the same set (without markers) as A4 has 64 states (use as check).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor guidance and extra-credit suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes for the instructor: project suitability, recommended student prerequisites, programmatic nature of tasks, and extra-credit suggestion to deduce sizes of smallest DFAs using Myhill–Nerode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as teaching notes: assign as a 3–4 week project in an advanced undergraduate/graduate class; expect students with ~2 years programming; offer extra credit requiring formal minimality proofs (Myhill–Nerode) for A1–A4 DFA sizes.
